title: Jennings v. Smith
description: Whether, under Ala. Code 1975, § 15-5-30, a law enforcement officer is prohibited from demanding or requesting physical identification when a person provides an incomplete or unsatisfactory oral response to a request for name, address, and explanation of actions.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the statute, by its plain text, does not permit law enforcement to demand physical identification.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the statute does not prohibit demanding physical identification and, in fact, empowers officers to demand it to affirmatively identify a suspect when oral responses are incomplete or unsatisfactory.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Alabama's "stop and identify" statute, § 15-5-30, does not prohibit a law enforcement officer from demanding physical identification when a suspect provides an incomplete or unsatisfactory oral response to verify their identity during a lawful Terry stop.

title: Crenshaw ex rel. Crenshaw v. Sonic Drive In of Greenville, Inc.
description: Whether the exclusive remedy provisions of the Alabama Workers' Compensation Act violate Article I, § 13, of the Alabama Constitution of 2022 by removing the mutual right for employers and employees to opt out of coverage, thereby denying a remedy by due process of law.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the Alabama Workers' Compensation Act is unconstitutional because it violates Article I, § 13, of the Alabama Constitution of 2022, as it no longer provides a mutual right for both employers and employees to opt out of coverage, thereby denying a remedy by due process of law.
defendant_argument: The defendant and the attorney general argued that the Alabama Workers' Compensation Act is constitutional and its exclusive remedy provisions validly bar the plaintiff's negligence action, as the legislature acted within its police power to eradicate a social evil.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment, ruling that the Alabama Workers' Compensation Act is constitutional and its exclusive-remedy provisions bar the plaintiff's negligence action.

title: LePage v. Center for Reproductive Medicine
description: Whether the Wrongful Death of a Minor Act applies to unborn children (embryos) located outside of a biological uterus, with plaintiffs arguing it does and defendants arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that the Wrongful Death of a Minor Act applies to all unborn children, including extrauterine embryos, and that denying this would create discontinuity in Alabama law and raise constitutional questions.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that an unborn child ceases to qualify as a 'child' or 'person' if not contained within a biological womb, and that public policy concerns like increased IVF costs should prevent such an interpretation.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's dismissal of the plaintiffs' wrongful-death claims, holding that the Wrongful Death of a Minor Act applies to all unborn children, including frozen embryos, and affirmed the dismissal of alternative negligence and wantonness claims as moot.

title: Belser v. Blount County
description: Whether the budget isolation resolution (BIR) for Act No. 2019-410 was passed in compliance with the constitutional requirement of 'not less than three-fifths of a quorum present', with the plaintiff arguing it was not constitutional due to insufficient votes, and the defendant arguing it is a nonjusticiable political question.
plaintiff_argument: Leah Abbott Belser argued that Act No. 2019-410 is unconstitutional because the budget isolation resolution (BIR) lacked sufficient favorable votes to comply with Amendment 448(C), which requires 'not less than three-fifths of a quorum present' of the members actually present and voting, contending that the House's interpretation was incorrect.
defendant_argument: Blount County argued that the question of how to determine what constitutes 'not less than three-fifths of a quorum present' is a nonjusticiable political question, relying on the separation of powers doctrine and the legislature's authority to determine its own rules of proceedings.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Alabama affirmed the trial court's judgment, concluding that the issue of whether the legislature conducted its internal voting proceedings in compliance with § 71.01 is a nonjusticiable political question.

title: Gulf Shores City Board of Education v. Mackey
description: Whether the local-tax act, which allocates sales tax proceeds for public education and other county services, is constitutional and whether its proceeds should be apportioned to include the Gulf Shores Board of Education.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that the local-tax act is unconstitutional because it does not apportion tax proceeds to the Gulf Shores Board of Education, violating state statutes requiring apportionment of county-wide education taxes and Article IV, Section 105 of the Alabama Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the local-tax act is constitutional, its plain language does not require apportionment to the Gulf Shores Board, and the court cannot rewrite the law to mandate such an allocation.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the circuit court's judgment dismissing the plaintiffs' claims, ruling that the local-tax act is constitutional and its proceeds are not allocable to the Gulf Shores Board of Education.

title: Dixon v. City of Auburn
description: Whether the City of Auburn's short-term-rental ordinance violates Steven Dixon's due process and equal protection rights, or if the City is equitably estopped from enforcing it.
plaintiff_argument: Dixon argued the short-term-rental ordinance violated his due process and equal protection rights, and that the City should be equitably estopped from enforcing it because his use was a preexisting nonconforming use and the City collected lodging taxes.
defendant_argument: The City argued the ordinance was valid, Dixon's short-term rental use was never a lawful, preexisting nonconforming use, and the doctrine of equitable estoppel did not apply.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's summary judgment in favor of the defendants, concluding that Dixon's claims regarding due process, equal protection, and equitable estoppel were unavailing.

title: Ex parte Warren Averett Cos.
description: Whether the contractual jury-trial waiver in a personal service agreement is enforceable, thereby striking the plaintiff's demand for a jury trial, or if the defendant's prior breach of the arbitration agreement invalidates the waiver and allows a jury trial.
plaintiff_argument: Fagan argued that Warren Averett's failure to pay arbitration fees constituted a breach, excusing her from the arbitration and jury-waiver provisions, and that the arbitration provision was not declared "unenforceable" as required for the waiver to apply, and that Warren Averett's motion to strike was barred by laches.
defendant_argument: Warren Averett argued that the jury-waiver provision was enforceable under the Gaylord factors, that its prior breach made the arbitration provision "unenforceable" triggering the jury waiver, and that Fagan's claims fell within the broad scope of the waiver, and that the motion was not barred by laches.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Alabama granted Warren Averett's petition for a writ of mandamus, directing the trial court to vacate its order denying Warren Averett's motion to strike Fagan's jury demand and to enter an order granting that motion.

title: Ex parte Pinkard
description: Whether State immunity and State-agent immunity bar Ronnie Taylor's lawsuit against State Deputy Fire Marshal Greg Pinkard for malicious prosecution and defamation.
plaintiff_argument: Taylor argued that his claims against Pinkard are not barred by State immunity and that Pinkard's eligibility for State-agent immunity involves disputed factual questions, urging the court to overrule the precedent set in Barnhart v. Ingalls.
defendant_argument: Pinkard argued that Taylor's claims are barred by State immunity and State-agent immunity, contending that his actions were within the scope of his official duties and should be treated as official-capacity claims under Barnhart's test.
decision_outcome: The court denied Pinkard's petition for a writ of mandamus, affirming the trial court's decision that Taylor's claims are not barred by State immunity and that Pinkard's State-agent immunity involves disputed factual questions, thus allowing Taylor's lawsuit to proceed.

title: Hawkins v. Ivey
description: Whether Alabama state officials had the legal authority to opt out of federal unemployment compensation programs, or if state immunity barred the lawsuit challenging that decision.
plaintiff_argument: The claimants argued that Alabama law did not permit Governor Ivey and Secretary Washington to opt Alabama out of federal unemployment compensation programs, imposing a legal duty to fully participate.
defendant_argument: Governor Ivey and Secretary Washington argued that the lawsuit was barred by the doctrine of State immunity and that the Governor has discretion to accept or decline federal funds.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Alabama affirmed the trial court's judgment, dismissing the claimants' lawsuit based on the doctrine of State immunity.

title: Glass v. City of Montgomery
description: Whether a municipal ordinance and a corresponding local act authorizing automated photographic enforcement of traffic-light violations violate sections 89, 104, and 105 of the Alabama Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the ordinance and local act violate state constitutional provisions by addressing matters already covered by general law, being inconsistent with general laws by effectively decriminalizing red-light running, and improperly fixing punishment for a crime.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the ordinance and local act are constitutional because they create a civil enforcement scheme not provided by general law, merely enlarge upon existing laws without inconsistency, and impose civil penalties rather than criminal punishment.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's judgment, upholding the constitutionality of the municipal ordinance and the local act.

title: Ex parte Jefferson County Board of Education
description: Whether the Jefferson County Board of Education is entitled to State immunity from suit under Section 14 of the Alabama Constitution, thereby requiring the dismissal of a breach of contract action against it.
plaintiff_argument: The Board is not entitled to State immunity, arguing that the precedent in Hale was misguided and should be overruled, and that State immunity under Section 14 should not immunize the State from contract claims.
defendant_argument: The Board is entitled to State immunity under Section 14 of the Alabama Constitution, which bars actions against State agencies, and therefore the lawsuit should be dismissed.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Alabama granted the Board's petition for a writ of mandamus, directing the circuit court to dismiss the action against the Board, affirming that the Board is entitled to State immunity.

title: Barnett v. Jones
description: Whether the 2019 local law appropriating Morgan County's Simplified Sellers Use Tax (SSUT) proceeds to education boards violates Ala. Const. 1901, art. IV, § 105.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Local Act is constitutional and does not violate § 105 because it addresses a distinct matter not already provided for by general law.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Local Act violates § 105 because it creates a variance from preexisting general laws (SSUT Act and Budget Control Act) and changes the results dictated by those laws.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's judgment, holding that the Local Act is constitutional and does not violate § 105.

title: Z.W.E. v. L.B. (Ex parte   Z.W.E.)
description: Whether the term "child," as used in § 26-17-204(a)(5) of the Alabama Uniform Parentage Act (AUPA), includes unborn children, thereby allowing an alleged biological father to establish paternity based on prebirth conduct.
plaintiff_argument: The alleged father argued that he is a presumptive father under the AUPA because he held out the child as his own since conception, provided financial and emotional support during pregnancy, and that the term "child" in the AUPA includes unborn children.
defendant_argument: The mother argued that the term "child" as defined in the AUPA does not include unborn children, meaning the alleged father cannot be a presumed father based on prebirth conduct, and that her husband is the presumed father.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Civil Appeals' decision, holding that the term "child" as defined in the AUPA does not include unborn children, thus the alleged father cannot be considered a presumed father based on prebirth conduct and lacked capacity to challenge the husband's paternity.

title: Butler v. Parks
description: Whether State immunity bars attorneys from recovering retrospective monetary relief for fees exceeding statutory caps for indigent defense, and whether attorneys have third-party standing to assert the constitutional rights of indigent defendants to a fair trial and effective assistance of counsel.
plaintiff_argument: The attorneys argued that State officials improperly refused to pay bills exceeding statutory caps, that the omission of a "good-cause exception" was a drafting error, and that the fee caps violate indigent defendants' constitutional rights to a fair trial and effective assistance of counsel.
defendant_argument: The State officials argued that State immunity bars the attorneys' claims for retrospective monetary relief and that the attorneys lack third-party standing to assert the constitutional rights of indigent defendants.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the trial court's class-certification order, ruling that State immunity bars the attorneys' claims for retrospective monetary relief and that the attorneys lack third-party standing to assert the constitutional rights of indigent defendants.
